The decision is a set of tradeoffs, and the volume, the data and the latency needs in the prompt each push in a direction. The most common mistake is to decide on one factor alone. Some candidates say "self-host, because health data must never leave the building" without checking whether a hosted API can offer acceptable contract terms, processing location and no retention. Others say "use the API, because it is cheaper" without asking whether the terms allow health data at all, which can rule the API out before cost matters.

A second mistake is to compare GPU rental with the API bill and stop there. A self-hosted model needs engineers to keep it running, patched and monitored, and at modest volume that cost often exceeds the hardware. The picture changes with scale. At 4,000 notes a day a GPU sits idle much of the time, but at many times that volume, or when several workloads share the hardware, self-hosting can win. A good answer says what would change the decision.
deeper: A strong candidate proposes a cheap experiment: run 200 real notes through both options, have clinicians score the summaries, and estimate monthly cost for each from measured token counts and GPU throughput. They might also put the model behind a common interface so the hospital can switch later without rewriting the feature.

subtopic: PII sent to an external API
prompt: A recruiting platform wants a third-party LLM API to summarize CVs for hiring managers. The CVs include names, phone numbers, home addresses and sometimes dates of birth. None of these are needed for a summary of skills and experience. What should the team do before sending CVs to the API?
options: Remove or replace the personal details first, and check how long the provider keeps inputs and whether it trains on them.
Encrypt each CV before it is sent, so the provider only stores ciphertext while the model still reads the content.
Send the CVs unchanged, since HTTPS already stops the provider from seeing, logging or keeping any of the content it receives.
Add an instruction to the prompt telling the model to forget the personal details once the summary has been written.
explanation:
Data minimization is the core privacy principle here. If the summary does not need a phone number or home address, those details should not leave your system. Redaction removes them, and pseudonymization swaps them for placeholders such as [CANDIDATE_1] that your own code can map back afterwards. Even then, a CV is still personal data, so you need to know the provider's terms: how long inputs and outputs are kept, whether they are used for training, who can access them and where they are processed.

Encryption does not work for this purpose. A model cannot read ciphertext, so whatever the provider decrypts to run the model is plain text on its side. HTTPS protects data while it travels over the network, but the provider receives the full content at the other end and may log or keep it. A prompt instruction to forget is meaningless. The model has no memory of the request to erase, and any retention happens in the provider's logs and storage, which a prompt cannot control.
deeper: Interviewers like to hear that a redactor is itself a model or rule set that can miss things, such as a phone number written with spaces or a name inside an email address. A strong answer adds tests for the redactor, a log of what was removed, and a review of the provider's terms before launch.

subtopic: explaining a RAG bot end to end
prompt: A product manager at an airline asks you to explain, in plain terms, how the new baggage-policy chatbot answers a customer's question, and where each step can go wrong. Give the explanation you would offer.
answer: Before any customer asks anything, we take the airline's baggage policy pages and cut them into short passages, each covering one rule. Each passage is turned into a list of numbers that captures its meaning and stored in a searchable index. When a customer asks a question, we turn it into numbers the same way and fetch the few passages whose meaning is closest. We hand those passages and the question to the language model, with an instruction to answer only from them and to cite them. Each step can fail. A page may be missing, outdated or badly extracted, for example a fee table that comes out jumbled. A rule can be split across two passages. The search can miss the right passage when the customer says "carry-on" and the policy says "cabin bag". And the model can ignore the passages, add details from its own memory, or answer when it should say it does not know.
points: Offline: policy pages split into passages, embedded and stored in an index
At question time: embed the question and fetch the closest passages
The model answers from those passages and cites them
Content failures: missing, outdated or badly parsed pages
Retrieval failures: rules split across passages, wording mismatch
Generation failures: ignoring the passages, inventing details, not declining
explanation:
The skill here is splitting the system into stages a non-specialist can follow, then tying each failure to a stage. That matters because fixes differ by stage. A wrong answer caused by an outdated page is fixed in the content pipeline, while one caused by the model ignoring a good passage is fixed in the prompt or the model choice.

The most common mistake is to describe the chatbot as "the AI reads all our policies and answers". That hides retrieval, which is where many real failures happen, and gives the manager no way to reason about errors. A second mistake is to bury the explanation in jargon such as embeddings, vector databases and top-k without saying what they do. The plain version, passages turned into numbers that capture meaning so similar text can be found, is accurate enough and easy to repeat. A third is to cover only the happy path. A manager mostly needs to know where it breaks and what the team can measure at each step.
deeper: A strong follow-up is to walk the manager through one real failure, such as a wrong pet-fee answer caused by a jumbled table, and show which stage caused it. Stakeholders trust a system more when they can see the team knows where its errors come from and how each one is measured.

subtopic: Q&A over a large document archive
prompt: An engineering firm has about one million PDFs from 20 years of projects: specifications with large tables, contracts, reports and scanned site notes. A few thousand files are added or revised each week. Engineers want to ask plain-language questions and get answers that cite the exact document and page. Design the system.
answer: Start with ingestion: a layout-aware parser for digital PDFs, OCR for scans, and table extraction that keeps headers with every row, flagging low-confidence pages. Chunk along document structure, such as sections and table blocks, and store metadata with each chunk: document ID, page, project, revision and date. Index each chunk twice, as an embedding in a vector database with approximate nearest neighbour search and in a BM25 keyword index, because engineers search for part numbers and clause codes that embeddings blur. At query time, run hybrid retrieval with metadata filters, rerank the top candidates with a cross-encoder, and have the model answer only from those chunks, citing document and page, with a check that each cited page exists and contains the quoted text. For freshness, run incremental ingestion that re-indexes changed files and removes superseded revisions. On cost, embedding a million documents is a one-off batch job, and the model sees only a few chunks per question. Enforce access permissions at retrieval, and track retrieval and citation quality on a test set.
points: Layout-aware parsing, OCR for scans, tables kept with their headers
Structure-based chunks with metadata: document, page, revision, date
Hybrid retrieval (vectors plus BM25) with filters and a reranker
Answers cite document and page, and the citations are checked
Incremental re-indexing that removes superseded revisions
Cost control, access permissions and a retrieval test set
explanation:
Much of the difficulty in this design sits before retrieval. A naive pipeline extracts raw text from every PDF and splits it into fixed-size chunks. Tables then become streams of numbers with no column names, scanned pages come out empty, and a value such as "rated load 40 kN" loses the row and column that gave it meaning. Parsing and structure-aware chunking set the ceiling for everything downstream.

The most common mistake is to rely on vector search alone. Engineering questions are full of exact identifiers, such as part numbers and standard codes, which dense embeddings often treat as near-misses. A keyword index catches these, and combining the two with a reranker covers both phrasing and exact terms. A second mistake is ignoring revisions. With weekly updates, an index that never removes old versions will cite a superseded spec, which can be worse than no answer. Third, citations must be checked, not just requested, since a model can cite a page that does not support the claim. Finally, access control belongs inside retrieval, because some contracts are restricted.
deeper: Interviewers often probe scale. A strong candidate estimates the index: a million documents at perhaps 50 chunks each is 50 million chunks, which calls for approximate search and possibly compressed vectors. They also keep the parsed text, so a future re-embedding run does not need to parse the PDFs again.

subtopic: rolling out a prompt or model change
prompt: Your team wants to move an email-drafting feature, used by 40,000 sales reps, to a newer and cheaper model with a reworked prompt. Plan the rollout so that a quality drop is caught before most reps see it, and so the change can be undone quickly.
answer: Treat the model and prompt as one versioned release behind a config flag. Offline, run the golden set of real drafting requests through the old and new versions and compare them with a pairwise LLM judge that has been checked against human ratings, plus checks for format, tone rules, latency and cost. Fix any category that regresses before going further. Next, run shadow traffic: send a copy of live requests to the new version without showing its drafts, and compare errors, latency and judge scores on real inputs. Then start a canary with 1 to 5% of reps chosen at random, and compare online signals with a control group on the old version: how often drafts are sent with few edits, regenerate clicks, complaints, latency and cost. Set pass and rollback thresholds before the canary starts. Ramp up in steps while the metrics hold. Rollback is a flag change back to the pinned old version, which stays deployed until the new one has run cleanly for a while.
points: Version the prompt and model together behind a flag
Offline golden set with a validated pairwise judge
Shadow traffic on live inputs without showing results
Small random canary compared with a control group
Online metrics: edits, regenerations, complaints, latency, cost
Thresholds set in advance and instant rollback to the pinned old version
explanation:
Each stage catches a different kind of problem at a different cost. Offline evals are cheap and fast but use a fixed set of inputs, so they miss what real traffic contains. Shadow traffic adds real inputs with no user risk, but shows nothing about how reps react. A canary measures real behaviour, such as whether reps send drafts or rewrite them, on a small share of users, so a problem reaches few people.

The most common mistake is to jump from a good offline score straight to full traffic. Golden sets rarely cover everything, and a cheaper model can fail on long threads or unusual languages that the set underrepresents. Another mistake is to decide the success bar after seeing the canary numbers, which makes it easy to explain away a drop. A third is a slow rollback that needs a new deploy, so the old version should stay live and switchable by config. Finally, the online comparison needs a control group on the old version at the same time, because day-to-day swings in email volume can hide or fake a change.
deeper: Interviewers may ask how long the canary should run. A strong answer ties it to sample size, meaning enough drafts to detect the smallest drop in send rate that matters, and to at least a full weekly cycle, since sales activity on a Monday differs from a Friday.

prompt: A job-matching site has 2 million job postings. A transformer encodes each posting into a vector once, offline, and stores it. When a candidate searches, the same kind of model encodes only the candidate's profile, and the site finds the nearest posting vectors. Because the query and each document are encoded separately and only meet as vectors at the end, this retrieval model is called a ______.
explanation:
A bi-encoder runs the query and the document through the encoder separately and compares the two vectors with a similarity score such as cosine. The key benefit is that document vectors do not depend on the query, so all 2 million postings can be encoded ahead of time. At search time the system encodes one profile and runs a fast nearest-neighbour search, which takes milliseconds.

The common wrong answer is "cross-encoder", which is the opposite design. A cross-encoder takes the query and one document together as a single input, so attention can link every word in one to every word in the other. That gives more accurate relevance scores, but nothing can be computed ahead of time, and scoring 2 million postings would need 2 million model passes per search. This is why the two are often combined: the bi-encoder fetches a shortlist, and a cross-encoder reranks it. "Embedding model" describes what a bi-encoder produces, not the design the question asks about, which is encoding the two sides separately.
deeper: Interviewers often ask how to make a bi-encoder more accurate without losing its speed. Good answers include fine-tuning it on your own query and match pairs, adding hard negatives that look relevant but are not, and putting a cross-encoder reranker on the top 50 to 100 results.

subtopic: a bot that cites outdated policy
prompt: A retailer's support bot uses RAG over its help-centre pages. It tells customers they have 30 days to return items, but the return window was cut to 14 days in March, and the new policy page went live that same day. Which of these could cause the bot's answer? Select all that apply.
options: The index has not been refreshed since before the change, so it holds only the old policy text and not the new page.
The old policy page was never deleted from the vector store, so both versions are indexed and the old one can be retrieved.
Retrieval has no filter or boost on effective date, so it has no reason to prefer the newer page when both match well.
The embedding model was trained before March, so it cannot represent text about a policy written after that date.
The index uses approximate nearest neighbour search, which favours vectors that were inserted earlier, such as the old page.
explanation:
A RAG bot can only be as current as what retrieval hands it, and three different gaps can each put the 30-day rule in front of the model. If the index has not been refreshed since the change, the new page was never embedded, so the old text is all retrieval can find. If the pipeline adds new pages but never removes replaced ones, both versions sit in the index. They describe the same topic in nearly the same words, so they score almost equally, and the old one can easily rank above the new one. Without a filter that keeps only current documents, or a boost for newer effective dates, nothing tips that tie toward the correct page.

The embedding model's training date does not matter here. It turns any text into a vector based on its words, and a sentence about a 14-day window is ordinary language it handles fine. What matters is whether that text was ever embedded. Approximate nearest neighbour search trades a little accuracy for speed, but it has no preference for older vectors. Insertion order does not make a vector more similar to the query.
deeper: The durable fix is a pipeline, not a one-off re-index. Each document carries an ID, a version and an effective date, an update replaces the old chunks for that ID, and retrieval filters to current versions. A strong candidate also adds a test case for each policy change, so the regression suite catches the bot quoting an old rule.

prompt: A legal search engine ranks documents by keyword match. A query term earns more credit the more often it appears in a document, but that credit rises toward a ceiling, so the tenth mention adds very little. Rare terms count more than common ones, and a tunable setting controls how much long documents are penalized for simply containing more words. This classic ranking function is called ______.
explanation:
BM25 scores a document by adding up a contribution for each query term, and each contribution has three parts. An inverse document frequency weight makes rare terms such as "indemnification" count more than common ones such as "agreement". A term frequency part grows with repeats but saturates, controlled by a parameter usually called k1, so a document cannot win by repeating one word fifty times. A length part, controlled by a parameter usually called b, compares the document's length with the average, so a long contract does not win just by containing more words.

The common wrong answer is TF-IDF. It shares the idea of rewarding frequent terms and weighting rare ones, but in its usual forms term frequency keeps growing without a ceiling, even when it is log-scaled, and there is no tunable length setting in the score. BM25 can be seen as a refined, better-behaved TF-IDF. Answering "cosine similarity" is also wrong. That compares two vectors and is not a keyword ranking function on its own.
deeper: BM25 is still a strong baseline and a standard part of hybrid search. It excels at exact terms that embeddings blur, such as case numbers, statute codes and product IDs, and it needs no training. A strong candidate adds that it misses synonyms, which is why it is paired with dense retrieval.
